caption:
Three Effingham County, Georgia, residents are suing OpenAI and local officials under the state's racketeering law over Project Camellia, a planned 3.2 gigawatt data center.
They say the deal was kept secret with nondisclosure agreements and closed-door meetings until it was done.
The complaint says about 1,440 acres were deeded to the company running the site for $10. These are allegations, not court findings.

Should towns get a vote before an AI data center moves in next door?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: WSB-TV, The Georgia Virtue, Tom's Hardware · Photo: WSB-TV
threads_text: OpenAI is being sued under Georgia's racketeering law by residents who say a $20 billion data center was pushed through in secret, with NDAs and closed-door votes. The complaint even says 1,440 acres were deeded for $10. Should neighbors get a vote before an AI data center moves in?

paragraphs.text: Three residents of Effingham County, Georgia, have sued OpenAI, county officials and the county's Industrial Development Authority over Project Camellia, a planned data center campus near Rincon, about 30 miles northwest of Savannah. The complaint was filed on November 6, 2026, and includes a claim under Georgia's Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act, WSB-TV reported on November 9.

The plaintiffs are Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver, according to The Georgia Virtue and Tom's Hardware. The defendants include OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the site for OpenAI, Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the development authority and its chief executive Brandt Herndon, County Manager Tim Callanan and six county commissioners.

Besides racketeering, the complaint alleges fraudulent concealment, fraud and misrepresentation, civil conspiracy and breach of legal duties. Lead attorney Ben Michaud of the Savage Turner firm called the case "a demand for transparency and accountability," WSB-TV reported, and the lawyers said the suit is not an attack on artificial intelligence itself.

According to The Georgia Virtue's account of the complaint, the development authority signed a nondisclosure agreement with OpenAI on October 27, 2025, roughly nine months before the project was announced. The suit says Herndon stated in April 2026 that the county was not recruiting data centers while he was in frequent contact with OpenAI.

The complaint says the authority met on July 21, 2026, on a date chosen by OpenAI, with an agenda that listed only "Project Gateway." After more than an hour in executive session, the board unanimously approved a memorandum of understanding. A July 24 deed then conveyed about 1,440 acres to Octans for $10, the suit says, and a zoning change adopted on August 4 let data centers proceed without conditional use hearings.

The suit also alleges that Georgia Power's economic development staff introduced OpenAI to the authority, and that commission chair Damon Rahn, who worked for Georgia Power, did not disclose that role or step aside. It describes a "Project Camellia Enterprise" operating from at least October 2025 through August 2026.

The memorandum of understanding describes a cumulative investment of $20 billion, and Tom's Hardware put the total at $20 billion to $30 billion across five phases. The campus could need up to 3.2 gigawatts of power, according to Inside Climate News, which compared that with about 1 gigawatt used by the city of Atlanta. Construction is set to begin in phases in 2028.

The authority approved a 50 percent property tax break for 15 years, which a lawsuit estimates could be worth nearly $900 million, Inside Climate News reported. OpenAI has said it will provide $80 million in community benefits, pay for the infrastructure upgrades the site needs and use a closed-loop cooling system to limit water use.

This is the third lawsuit over Project Camellia. The same three residents challenged the county's zoning ordinance in September, and later that month the Southern Environmental Law Center sued on behalf of the conservation group One Hundred Miles and five residents, asking a court to void the tax abatement and the land sale, WTOC reported.

The new complaint asks for a jury trial, compensatory and punitive damages, and three times actual damages under the RICO claim. The plaintiffs say nearby home buyers lowered or withdrew offers after the project was announced. The claims are allegations that have not been tested in court, and none of the outlets reported a response from OpenAI or the county.

The case turns a common complaint about data centers, that neighbors learn about them only after the deals are signed, into a fraud and racketeering fight. By pleading a racketeering claim, the plaintiffs are treating a series of separate local approvals as one coordinated scheme, and whether a judge accepts that framing is the first real test of the suit.
The next step is how OpenAI, Octans and the county respond in court, and whether a judge lets the racketeering claim proceed alongside the open meetings challenges already pending.
